name: Piglet Wardriver
firmware_note: One codebase built for four different Seeed XIAO targets (ESP32-S3, C5, C6, C3); board choice decides whether you get 5GHz. Adds an ESP-NOW mesh scanning-node mode not found in most older wardriving firmware.
price_note: Cost of a bare Seeed XIAO ESP32-C5 board only (needed for the 5GHz feature). Add roughly $10-20 for a UART GPS module, a few dollars for an optional OLED and an SD card - a real 5GHz-capable build runs closer to $35-50 all in, not $14.
skill_note: Flashing is simple, but there is no official carrier board - you wire your own GPS module (and optionally an OLED) to a bare XIAO before it is a wardriver at all.
build_note: No official kit or enclosure. You supply the XIAO board and a UART GPS module and wire them yourself; the README mentions a PCBWay pre-assembled listing but that is third-party, not official.
summary: Open-source wardriving firmware for Seeed's XIAO ESP32 family: 2.4GHz Wi-Fi scanning on every supported board, genuine 5GHz scanning on the C5, GPS-tagged WiGLE-format CSV logging to SD, a live web UI, and an ESP-NOW mesh mode letting several units share scan coverage as networked nodes. It is a passive collection tool with no attack features anywhere in the source.
honest_take: Piglet does one job and is honest that it only does that job - there is no deauth, no injection, nothing offensive in the source, and it is entitled to the credit that deserves. The catch is what the $14 headline price hides: that is a bare MCU board with no GPS, no case, and no carrier PCB, so a real build costs closer to $35-50 once you wire in a GPS module yourself. If you want 5GHz wardriving without any DIY wiring, the already-tracked C5 Wardriver (also ESP32-C5-based, from the ESP32 Marauder author) ships as a proper host board with GPS, battery management, a screen and buttons built in for $69 plus a $10-15 dev kit - more total dollars, zero soldering. Piglet's actual differentiator is the ESP-NOW mesh mode, which nothing else in this comparison offers, and the CC BY-NC license means nobody can legally sell you a finished unit even if they wanted to.

name: ESP8266 Deauther
firmware_note: The direct conceptual ancestor of ESP32 Marauder and most of the deauther firmware in this comparison. Still receiving issues and pull requests into 2025 despite a last code commit of 2024-08-14 - unusually long-lived for a single-maintainer ESP project.
price_note: Cost of a bare Wemos D1 Mini or NodeMCU ESP8266 board - no official kit or case exists. Pre-flashed boards sold by unrelated third parties on marketplaces run closer to $20.
skill_note: Flash-and-go on a $6 board over USB; no soldering for basic use, though the optional OLED/TFT display and button add-ons are a separate wiring step.
build_note: Arduino IDE flash to any ESP8266 board. Optional display and physical buttons are documented but sold/sourced separately.
summary: The firmware that effectively founded the ESP-based Wi-Fi attack category: deauthentication flooding, beacon/SSID spam, and Wi-Fi scanning on a sub-$10 ESP8266 board, with a web UI and an optional physical display. It has no Bluetooth, no 5GHz, and no packet injection beyond management-frame attacks - 2017-era ESP8266 capability, not the newer ESP32/C5 feature set found elsewhere in this batch.
honest_take: This is the firmware essentially every other ESP-based deauther and Marauder-style tool descends from conceptually, and it is still maintained nearly a decade later - genuinely unusual longevity for this category. But do not confuse 'foundational' with 'capable': the ESP8266 has no Bluetooth radio at all, no 5GHz, and PMF/802.11w defeats its deauth exactly as it defeats every newer device's deauth, on any modern access point. If you want the same basic idea with a screen, GPS, BLE and an actively maintained community, ESP32 Marauder (already tracked at multiple price points from $20 up) picked up where this project left off and is the better buy for anything built after about 2019.

honest_take: This is the same firmware documented in detail on the already-tracked bare-CYD HaleHound entry, and every caveat there applies here too: it is marketed in places as open source and is not - the firmware repo holds only a README and a proprietary license, no code, and that license explicitly forbids redistribution or modification. summary: A retro-gaming-styled ESP8266 handheld (1.44in 128x128 color TFT, 8 buttons, speaker, RGB LED) built around a standardized expansion connector. On its own it is a Little Game Engine console; plugging in separate modules adds Wi-Fi attacks, RFID/NFC read/write/clone/emulate, iButton storage, 433MHz garage/barrier control, GPS, LoRa, and BadUSB-style payloads. Fully open source and OSHWA-certified.
honest_take: The gaming branding is doing real work to disguise a genuinely capable multi-protocol platform, and that cuts both ways. As a stealth angle, nothing about this looks like a hacking tool, which is a real advantage over an overtly 'pentest' branded handheld. But 'multi-protocol capability bolted onto a retro-gaming platform' undersells how much extra buying is required: the base $79 unit does none of the RF/RFID/BadUSB tricks by itself - every one of those needs its own separate module purchase, and the ESP8266 at the core has no Bluetooth and no native USB, so any 'BadUSB' claim for this platform almost certainly means a separate USB-capable companion board rather than the ESP8266 itself emulating a keyboard. It is the most genuinely open-source device in this whole batch (OSHWA RU000001, full schematics and code per module on GitHub), which deserves real credit - but only 1 unit was in stock at last check, so availability is a live concern.
